Field note · Tāmaki Makaurau

12 OCTOBER 2026

On learning the names
of things, slowly

A fern I’ve passed for years, a new word, and the kind of attention that only arrives when we stop pretending to know.

fernlearningfield notes
On this pageA name as a doorThe practice of returningEnough to begin

Some names arrive like doors. You hear one, and a thing that was merely green becomes particular: a shape with habits, a history, a preferred kind of shade. I used to think that learning a name was the finish of an encounter. More and more, it feels like the beginning.

On the path behind the community hall there is a fern I’ve walked past for years. It occupies the small wet seam between a retaining wall and a row of pōhutukawa. I noticed it mostly as texture—the soft persistence of green where the concrete said nothing should grow.

⌁FIELD SKETCH · NOT TO SCALE · 12 OCT 2026

The practice of returning

This week I came back with a notebook. Not to collect a fact, exactly, but to hold the question open. The fronds were narrower than I remembered; the new growth arrived furled like a small shoulder. A nearby person mentioned a name, and the fern stepped out of the background.

Knowing the name did not make the fern more valuable. It made my attention less casual.

There is a useful humility in the slowness of this. A field guide can offer a possibility, but the place has the last word. Light changes, leaves age, and sometimes the honest record is simply: returned three times, still learning.

Enough to begin

Perhaps we don’t need to know everything to be responsible to what we meet. A name can be a handle, not a possession. It gives us a way to ask better questions, to look for kin, to notice when something is absent.

So I’m keeping this entry unfinished. Next time I pass that wall, I’ll stop again. There may be a better name. There may be a story. Either would be enough to begin.
